notes: High-confidence opposing pollinator and seed-predator selection anchor; do not call effect-size ready until component uncertainty/covariance is recovered.
Path-decomposed common seed-fitness result is biologically strong but not automatically coefficient-compatible with standardized beta estimates.
Fourteen populations remain one literature cluster; geographic variation is moderator structure rather than independent-study replication.

Pollination and herbivory were factorially manipulated; pollinators selected for later flowering and herbivores for earlier flowering with similar additive strength. Appendix A2 reports beta plus SE for all four treatment groups but agent-effect covariance or interaction uncertainty must be reconstructed before effect-size readiness.

Source-reported mediated contrasts are P|Hpresent=-0.022±0.314; P|Habsent=0.572±0.224; H|open=-0.391±0.125; H|supplemented=0.203±0.365. Table S2 also reports OP-HA=0.181±0.213 and Table S3 reports the inflorescence-density Pollination×Herbivory interaction F=2.366. The factorial identities plus the 1-df F uniquely reconstruct the full rank-3 joint covariance; no zero-covariance assumption is used.

HCN x pollination x herbivory factorial with public clean data and R code. Pollination did not independently alter selection on any trait; herbivory changed selection on inflorescence production and HCN-modified flower traits. Keep as a design-matched negative control rather than a Q1B positive.

Four-site field experiment identifies strict opposing selection on one genetically based display dimorphism. Keep the long-vs-short relative-fitness estimand separate from continuous standardized beta and from the four-context Q1B contrast vector.

Pollinator-mediated delta beta is -0.01±0.05 for inflorescence number; 0.00±0.06 for height; -0.07±0.06 for flowering start. Pollination x damage x trait contrasts are -0.12±0.12; 0.11±0.13; 0.01±0.12. Herbivory changes direct selection but does not generate a diffuse opposing Q1B pair.
Corolla width has strong pollination selection but no detected seed-predation selection in the same dataset; preserve as a boundary/control rather than forcing conflict.

Methods audit shows no florivore or insect-herbivore damage in the focal population; authors state antagonistic interactions are unlikely to explain the opposing nonpollinator-mediated gradients and suggest resource limitation or unmeasured correlated traits instead.

Pollination and nectar robbing both contribute to selection on some traits but direction and intensity vary between years; extract trait-year path effects before assigning opposed versus aligned status.

Seed predators mediate spatially variable selection on inflorescence height and flower number across 44-52 populations over two years; a matched pollinator-mediated coefficient is not supplied by this source alone.

Inflorescence height increases fruit/seed set but decreases escape from seed predation; this is a strong component conflict but fertilization success is not an experimentally isolated pollinator beta.

Tubular manipulation reduces ant entry but also pollen receipt and seed set; the source supports upgrading the existing Polemonium R-layer conflict pattern but is not a standardized beta pair for Q1 pooling.
